en: The Sutra of Ānanda’s Seven Dreams, translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Tanwulan of India during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
While Ānanda was in Śrāvastī, he had seven kinds of dreams and came to question the Buddha about them. The first was:
First, the flames of the ponds and pools surge up to the heavens;
second, he dreams that the sun and moon set, and the stars likewise vanish;
third, he dreams that a renunciant bhikṣu is turned upside down within an impure pit and ditch, while a layperson in white robes climbs over his head and emerges.
Fourth, he dreamed that a herd of pigs came to butt and trample a sandalwood grove, which he found strange;
fifth, he dreamed that he wore Mount Sumeru upon his head, yet did not consider it heavy;
sixth, he dreamed that a great elephant abandoned a small elephant.

Seventh, he dreams of a lion king named Huasa, with seven tufts of hair upon its head, lying dead upon the ground; all birds and beasts see it and are terrified, but later they see worms emerge from within its body, which they then devour.
He came to ask the Buddha about this evil dream.
At that time, the Buddha was at the Puhui Hall in Śrāvastī, preaching the Dharma to King Prasenajit:
that suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation constitute true happiness.
Seeing Ānanda’s sorrowful countenance and his inexpressible grief and suffering, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
“As for these dreams, they all pertain to the future five-turbulence evil world; they shall not harm you. Why do you show such a sorrowful countenance?”
"The first dream:
'The flames of a pond and lake surge up to the heavens.

This signifies that in the future, the virtuous minds of bhikṣus will diminish, while wickedness and rebellion will blaze forth, such that they will slaughter one another in numbers beyond reckoning."
"The second dream:
the sun and moon set, and the constellations also vanished.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the śrāvakas followed him into parinirvāṇa and no longer remain in the world; the eyes of sentient beings have been extinguished."
"The third dream:
A renunciant bhikṣu was situated within a pit of impurity, while a layperson in white robes climbed onto his head and emerged.

This signifies that in the future, bhikṣus will harbor poison and jealousy, leading to mutual slaughter. A practitioner will sever their heads, and while the layperson in white robes looks on, they will fail to heed his admonitions and rebukes; consequently, they will die and fall into hell."
"Those laypeople who practice with diligence will be reborn in the heavens after death.
As for the fourth dream:
that a herd of pigs came to butt and trample the sandalwood grove—this is a portent."
"In the future, laypeople will enter monasteries and pagodas, slandering the Sangha, seeking out their faults, destroying pagodas, and harming monks.
'The fifth dream was:
wearing Mount Sumeru upon one's head, yet not considering it heavy.'"

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda shall serve as the master for the compilation of the sūtras by the thousand arhats; he will not forget a single word, and having received many realizations, he will not consider this a heavy burden.
"The sixth dream:
a great elephant abandons its young.
In the future, false views will blaze forth, destroying my Buddha-dharma, and those of virtuous character will all remain hidden and not appear."
"The seventh dream:
the death of the lion.
One thousand four hundred and seventy years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, my disciples who cultivate a heart of virtue shall not be disturbed by any evil Māras."
"The 'Seven Hairs' refers to events occurring seven hundred years later.
— *Ānanda-saptasvapna-sūtra* (The Sutra of Ānanda’s Seven Dreams)
